prompt: Why is a world-writable script run by root's cron a path to root?

choices.text: Because cron runs every script with a shell that has no password
choices.why: The danger is who can change the script, not the shell.

choices.text: What root runs next is any account's to rewrite tonight
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Because world-writable files are executed twice
choices.why: Nothing runs them twice.

choices.text: Because cron refuses to log scripts with those bits
choices.why: cron logs normally; logging is not the issue.

prompt: What does `sudo -u portal test -w /opt/portal/backup.sh` answer, and what does it change?

choices.text: Whether ana may write the file; it changes its owner to portal
choices.why: It runs as portal, and changes nothing.

choices.text: Whether the file is executable; it marks it as tested
choices.why: -w asks about writing; nothing is marked.

choices.text: Whether portal may write it, and nothing changes
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Whether portal wrote to it recently; it resets the timestamp
choices.why: test asks about permission, not history.

prompt: What does `find / -perm -4000` look for?

choices.text: Files that run with their owner's privilege
choices.why: Right: the set-user-id bit.

choices.text: Files larger than 4000 bytes in the root file system
choices.why: -perm is about mode bits, not size.

choices.text: Directories anybody may write without the sticky bit
choices.why: That is another search with other bits.

choices.text: Files that every user may read but nobody may write
choices.why: 4000 is the set-user-id bit.

prompt: Why can the nine bits not give the auditor read-only access to a file the accountants write?

choices.text: Because read and write cannot be separated in the bits
choices.why: They are separate bits.

choices.text: They name one owner and one group, and both slots are taken
choices.why: Right. Other would give it to everybody.

choices.text: Because auditors are not allowed accounts on Linux
choices.why: She has one, auditoria.

choices.text: Because the set-group-id bit forbids extra readers
choices.why: It only sets the group of new files.

prompt: What does the `+` after the bits in `ls -l` mean?

choices.text: The file is larger than the block size
choices.why: ls shows size elsewhere.

choices.text: The file has the sticky bit set
choices.why: That shows as t in the bits.

choices.text: The file was changed since the last backup
choices.why: ls knows nothing of backups.

choices.text: More access exists than the bits show
choices.why: Right: an ACL.

prompt: Why does the auditor need `rx` on the directory as well as `r` on the file?

choices.text: x enters the directory, r lists it
choices.why: Right. Without x the file is unreachable.

choices.text: Because files inherit the directory's entries when read
choices.why: Entries are inherited only at creation, by defaults.

choices.text: Because cat executes the file it reads
choices.why: cat reads; it does not execute.

choices.text: Because the mask on the directory is rwx
choices.why: The mask limits; it does not require.

prompt: On a file with a named entry `user:portal:rw-`, an administrator runs `chmod 640`. What can portal do now?

choices.text: Read and write, because its own entry still says rw-
choices.why: The entry is capped by the mask.

choices.text: Nothing, because chmod removes every ACL entry
choices.why: The entries remain; getfacl lists them.

choices.text: Read only: chmod set the mask to r--
choices.why: Right. The middle bits of ls are the mask.

choices.text: Write only, because the group bits became r--
choices.why: The mask allows r, not w.

prompt: Why does the mask exist at all?

choices.text: To store the owning group's permissions in a second place
choices.why: It caps entries; it is not a copy.

choices.text: So nine-bit tools still narrow a file that has an ACL
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: To hide the ACL from users who are not root
choices.why: Anybody may read it with getfacl where they can reach the file.

choices.text: To make files inherit their directory's entries
choices.why: That is the default ACL.

prompt: On a file marked `+`, where do you read the access people actually have?

choices.text: In the middle three bits of ls -l
choices.why: Those are the mask.

choices.text: In getfacl's #effective column, beside each entry
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: In /etc/group, next to each member's name
choices.why: Groups list members, not file access.

choices.text: In the file's own first line
choices.why: Content says nothing about access.

prompt: After `setfacl -d` on /srv/clientes, the auditor still cannot read costa.txt. Why?

choices.text: Defaults apply only to files created by root
choices.why: souza.txt was created by maria and got them.

choices.text: The default needs a reboot to take effect
choices.why: It applied to the next file at once.

choices.text: A default applies at creation, and costa.txt already existed
choices.why: Right. setfacl -R -m fixes what exists.

choices.text: Because joao's umask overrides any default ACL
choices.why: A default ACL replaces the umask for new files.

prompt: A document is moved with `mv` from a user's home into /srv/clientes on the same file system. What ACL does it have?

choices.text: The one it had in the home
choices.why: Right. A move creates nothing, so no default applies.

choices.text: The directory's default, because it now lives there
choices.why: Defaults apply at creation only.

choices.text: None: mv strips every ACL
choices.why: It keeps the file's attributes.

choices.text: The union of both
choices.why: Nothing merges lists.

prompt: The auditor joins contabil, which has rw-, but keeps her named entry r--. She asks to write. What happens?

choices.text: Allowed: her group grants write, and access is added up
choices.why: Linux never adds entries up.

choices.text: Refused: her named entry is found first
choices.why: Right. Step 2 stops before groups are asked.

choices.text: Allowed once, then refused until she logs in again
choices.why: The answer is the same every time.

choices.text: Refused, because members of contabil may only read
choices.why: contabil may write; joao did.

prompt: Maria owns silva.txt. Which entry decides what she may do with it?

choices.text: The group entry, because she is in contabil
choices.why: Ownership is checked before groups.

choices.text: The mask, which limits everybody
choices.why: The owner is outside the mask.

choices.text: The owner entry, user::
choices.why: Right, and nothing else is looked at.

choices.text: Whichever of her entries grants the most
choices.why: Entries are not compared or summed.

prompt: On NTFS, a group has an explicit deny for write and a user in it has an explicit allow. Can the user write?

choices.text: Yes, because the user's own entry is more specific
choices.why: That is Linux's rule, not NTFS's.

choices.text: No: at the same level, deny is evaluated first
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Only if inheritance is broken on the folder
choices.why: Both entries are explicit; inheritance is not involved.

choices.text: Yes, if the user logs in after the deny was written
choices.why: Timing does not change evaluation order.

prompt: In `icacls D:\Clientes /grant "JATOBA\Auditoria:(OI)(CI)R"`, what do (OI)(CI) do?

choices.text: Grant ownership and full control
choices.why: R is read; OI and CI are inheritance.

choices.text: Remove all inherited entries from the folder
choices.why: That is /inheritance:r.

choices.text: Make the entry flow down to files and subfolders
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Limit the grant to the folder itself
choices.why: They do the opposite.
